item.title: VR Goggles Get Dual Use for Suicide Prevention, Counter-drone Training

item.content:encoded:
CAMP PENDLETON, Calif. — The global proliferation of cheap, small unmanned aerial systems that threaten troops has military services racing to incorporate counter-drone training as a top combat readiness priority.

In 2025, the 1st Marine Logistics Group’s Headquarters and Service Battalion purchased a virtual-reality goggles kit for its Marines and sailors to learn how to neutralize drones. Around the same time, the battalion was focusing on building resiliency and force readiness. Trainers soon realized the VR technology had other uses.

The VR goggles use software modules that integrate AI to give users a realistic experience in an immersive digital environment. In a counter-drone scenario, small squads can work together to neutralize threatening drones. In a suicide prevention scenario, the user can talk and interact directly with someone – in such cases, an upset “AI” avatar who responds and reacts physically to whatever the user says.

For H&S Battalion, the dual use of the VR system – goggles from contractor OperatorXR and counter-drone and suicide prevention training modules from Moth+Flame – is a double win. The battalion began incorporating the VR tech into suicide prevention training over the summer, as well as leadership courses at Combat Skills Training School and its Counter Small UAS Course.

The VR system’s suicide prevention module puts users through conversations so they can practice how to respond and handle what can be tough, highly personal or volatile situations with their peers and subordinates.

“Now you have to think as an individual and as a leader what is the best answer to their question, or what is the best statement to that individual,” said Sgt. Maj. Brian Price, the battalion’s senior enlisted leader told USNI News last month. “It really prompts the thought process.”

The goggles have small microphones and surround-sound speakers that amplify the sense of a physical environment. The AI actor, scenario and environment can be tailored to an intended story line and training objective.

“There’s an operator, someone that’s a combat operation type of individual that’s been overseas… or a support role individual that works in-house, not necessarily deployed yet but going through some problems,” Price said.

The user chooses from a series of prompts to drive the conversation with the agitated AI Marine or sailor, and it ends with a feedback review they can later discuss with instructors. The goal is to de-escalate the situation, temper high emotions and encourage the distressed person to get to safety and accept help.

“It engages how you respond and it gives you that feedback, ‘Okay, maybe I can do better on responding to someone in need’,” he said.

Battalion leaders see the VR tech as helping prompt and ease Marines and sailors into becoming more comfortable and confident in uncomfortable talks about their life’s stressors or problems or suicidal thoughts. Most noncommissioned officers have likely never had to do that, Price said.

“They’ve never had to sit in front of someone and say, ‘Hey, you need help, let’s get you help.’ It gives them essentially a reference set on how to do that,” Price said.

In MLG’s suicide prevention training, students apply what they learn from PowerPoint briefing slides, class discussions and one-on-one role play into flowing conversations with the AI actor who reacts and responds.

“We all want to tell each other, ‘it’s okay to ask for help. You can ask for help anytime,’ and we want to offer help,” said Lt. Col. Gloria Luedtke, the H&S Battalion commander. “Then when it gets to that point, we’re like, all right, we’ve identified there’s a problem. A Marine needs to talk to someone. I’m that Marine. I’m this Marine’s roommate, and I am a 19-year-old lance corporal who has had no experience talking about stuff like suicide. That’s a heavy topic.”

The scenarios vary. In one scenario, the user is the concerned roommate of a lance corporal despondent – and potentially suicidal or prone to harmful behaviors – over a failed relationship and punishment by his unit.

As the user begins conversing with the despondent “actor” – microphones in the VR headsets pick up their voice – the integrated AI offers several potential responses, of which, one is the preferred response to convince the Marine to accept help. The virtual environment also varies; in one scenario, the Marine was met first in their home garage and then seated in their private room.

Depending on the chosen responses, the situation can escalate into serious concern over self-harm. The Marine may become agitated and curse at the user, for example, or the situation is de-escalated into choosing help from the user or others.

“You have to think as an individual and as a leader what is the best answer to their question or what is the best statement to that individual,” said Luedtke. “It really prompts the thought process for the person.”

H&S Battalion demonstrated the system at a recent commanders’ conference at Camp Pendleton but got tepid interest from the more-senior officers and enlisted leaders, she said. “But at the end of the conference, we had units reach out and say, we’d like to get that over here,” Luedtke said.

Survivability is a Training Priority

Brig. Gen. Omar Randall began a modernization push across 1st MLG in 2025 that continues today. H&S Battalion bought 20 OperatorXR sets with counter-drone training in mind for $200,000, intending to test and weigh its training benefits, Luedtke said.

The VR environment lets Marines and sailors get the sensory feel and experiences of stress, fear and multi-tasking under fire, logical training needed to defend against today’s drone threats. Then this year, H&S Battalion established its Counter-sUAS Course taught by its Combat Skills Training School, which is open to all MLG and I Marine Expeditionary Force units.

“Logistics is always the number one target, so we are focused on survivability,” Luedtke said. “When we go forward, we are always vulnerable… as the enemy’s priority target,” she said. “Our priority is to protect ourselves and defend ourselves… to be able to carry out our mission to support the warfighters.”

In July, the battalion began using the suicide prevention module over two training days during its Small Unit Leadership Course that teaches mentorship and coaching for lieutenants, staff sergeants and warrant officers. The training is in line with I Marine Expeditionary Force’s “Never Fight Alone” campaign and resilience.

“We always want the Marines to learn resilience by sending the message, Just Fight. Fight all the time,” Luedtke said.

The idea to incorporate the VR goggles into leadership courses came from Maj. Paul Kim, H&S Battalion’s executive officer. Kim plans to get at least 1,000 Marines trained in the suicide prevention module this year. With strong initial interest – some 350 were already trained as of mid-October – he’s upping that goal and extending it to Corporal’s Courses, Lance Corporal Seminars and Small Unit Leadership Courses around I MEF.

Before using the VR goggles, Kim said, Marines and sailors learn about the concept of emotional intelligence, hard conversations, coaching, mentoring and counseling.

“This is actually a great segue to really kind of seal the deal… to having conversations with another Marine,” Kim said.

In his prior tour as a U.S. Naval Academy teacher in the Stockdale Center, Kim taught leadership and ethics to midshipmen and saw a demonstration of the OperatorXR’s VR headset. Last year, as battalion operations officer, he began working with Combat Skills Training School on counter-drone training. He said he realized the interactive OperatorXR system used by Marine Corps Special Operations Command could help with leadership, mental health and other issues including suicide prevention.

Tackling Tough Talk in Training

Suicide prevention instruction is tailored to the rank.

“For the lance corporals, you’re likely going to have hard conversations with other lance corporals, so that the dynamics are different,” Kim said.

Older non-commissioned officers might have more experiences and awareness to be more empathetic in having those hard conversations.

Students can benefit from real scenarios that aren’t just about suicide, he said, such as someone debating whether to reenlist or grappling with a lost love or struggling with their weight and fitness.

“Then we had some ethical scenarios of a Marine going towards the wrong path and bad decision-making. How do you encourage that Marine to get back onto the right path and help calibrate his moral compass towards the right direction?” said Kim, on a break last month instructing a class of 66 small unit leaders.

Prompts in the VR scenarios help guide decisions – right or wrong – and more learning than just role playing where some students take it less seriously.

“I’ll get feedback from them and see what they say,” he said. “More often than not, they’re telling me the right answers. But the fact that they’re discussing with each other… and disagreeing with one another and brought it to a solution, I think that’s really important.”

The goal is for students to teach their junior Marines and NCOs and impact some to step up to help when needed, he added.

For 2nd Lt. Luke Enriquez, the training brought more realism to instruction about handling tough topics he got at The Basic School.

“We’ve been given the tools as to how you should respond but never actually played out,” said Enriquez, a manpower officer with 1st MLG G-1 Administration. “[For some questions], I thought, that is a good response I would use if I ever was presented with this.”

Enriquez said he’s had more discussions about mental health since doing I MEF’s “Tomahawk 22” mile hike encouraging resiliency.

“Just really having that conversation, just being open about it – especially as small unit leaders – enables us to go into such a conversation, not blind but with some things in our back pocket we can use,” he said.

Conversations with the AI actor challenged students’ notions of what to do and how to react, especially when personal situations become uncomfortable.

“I definitely questioned myself a lot more than I thought,” said 2nd Lt. Rylee Rives, logistics officer with Combat Logistics Battalion 5. “There was a lot of push back. I did not expect that at all… That’s definitely prepared me for the future.”

The ability to interact and get feedback on decision points sets this training apart, Rives told USNI News.

“This is something that we are facing today, right now, as second lieutenants who are the closest officers to the junior enlisted and to enlisted Marines,” she said. “This is on us to be able to have these conversations and take it seriously.”

Sgt. Julian McCoy, a logistics specialist with Combat Logistics Regiment 1, said he appreciated the training’s realism.

“It’s really helpful to put Marines in a position… who maybe haven’t been in that predicament to point them in the right direction… to get the Marines the help they need,” McCoy said.

Sgt. Michael Mathis, a combat engineer with 7th Engineer Support Battalion, said being put into uncomfortable situations was important.

“Actually seeing how tough that conversation is with the questions that you’re asked, it really makes you think,” Mathis said.

The training got students thinking about leadership and rank differences and interacting with subordinates outside of work. Having a healthy balance might help when small-unit leaders face tough personal or professional situations.

“I’m always there for my Marines and they understand that, and even away from this rank, you’re always going to be my brother and sister and I think of you as such,” McCoy said.

Rather than avoid having that hard conversation – like thinking a Marine who got a DUI will “just deal with it,” he said – leaders instead should try peeling back that layer, and maybe just have a conversation.

McCoy detailed a conversation he had with a junior Marine that he picked up from jail for suspected driving under the influence. McCoy offered his encouragement to the Marine, telling him that while a mistake was made, it wasn’t the end of the world – using what the VR training teaches.

“It’s not looking at them like they’re trash because they messed up…I told him, you know you’re young, this isn’t the end of the world. You’re gonna see the consequences of it,” McCoy said.

Immersed in the Environment

The same VR goggles that enable suicide prevention training are bringing counter-drone training indoors.

First MLG’s counter-drone course and outdoor range established earlier this year at Camp Pendleton teaches Marines and sailors how to detect, defend and defeat – and how to hide from adversary drones, too.

Now OperatorXR’s OP-2 Interceptor counter sUAS VR training kit, which fits into a portable hardened case, lets them practice indoors. Trainers – a combination of Marines and OperatorXR contractors – build the scenarios, often taking the page from news headlines and after-action reports from Ukraine, the Middle East and elsewhere.

With the kit, trainers can build the virtual “physical” environment – be it an office, warehouse, gymnasium or a ship’s hangar bay – and turn it into a battlefield scene, with trenches, bunkers, camouflage netting and trees. That physical VR environment can be small or large and accommodate two or more users, such as a mock fire team or squad.

With goggles and small devices that represent their issued rifle or pistol weapon, users immerse themselves as first-person shooters into the virtual battlefield in the hunt to find, identify and neutralize enemy drones while also fending off enemy combatants.

Marines and sailors are placed in a Ukrainian war-torn environment, where they have to run around, hide around corners and shoot down drones, Kim said.

“There’s a true psychological benefit to this type of training, because in VR, I’m actually seeing combative threats. I’m actually hearing it. My heart rate is going up. I’m scared to go around the corner,” Kim said.

The training is not scripted like field training. The newest training will incorporate chemical, biological, radiological and nuclear (CBRN) scenarios.

“We’re learning that it’s a lot more realistic immersive training through VR and actually gives you the reps and sets of your MOS before you actually have to do it in real life,” Kim said.

For Marines who are gamers but less familiar with drones or close-quarters battle, doing a counter-sUAS mission in a virtual space caught their curiosity.

Cpl. Nicholas Muldrow, a supply administrator with H&S Battalion, likened it to skeet shooting.

“I was hoping to learn more about how the drones operate. One of the CSTS Marines said it kind of flies up and then down directly at you. That’s something I definitely didn’t know before,” Muldrow said.

“The repetitions, especially when it comes to CQB training or room clearing, is definitely going to benefit a lot of Marines,” Muldrow said. “In real life, you can’t adjust a scenario before you walk into actual combat. I think throwing Marines into different situations and having them rely on their instincts and their buddy is really good training.”
Cpl. Austin Miller, a supply administrator, said it took a moment to orient himself because through the VR goggles, users can see their weapons and their hands.

“With the new technology the Marine Corps is getting, training like this is exactly what I was hoping to get,” Miller said. “Because as supply Marines, there’s not too much combat training that we get. This is definitely something that we can be involved in and learn a lot from.”

And when they deploy, they will have their bearings.

“They’re not just standing there scared,” he said.

item.content:encoded:
The following is the Nov. 4, 2026, Congressional Research Service report, Golden Dome: Potential Strategic Stability Considerations for Congress.

From the Report

The second Trump Administration has proposed to develop a “next-generation missile defense shield” against nuclear and conventional attacks that it has called a “Golden Dome for America.” Since the 1950s, Members of Congress have periodically debated the costs, feasibility, scope, and sufficiency of strategic defense systems that could limit damage to the U.S. homeland from a nuclear attack. In these debates, some Members have stated that some of these systems could adversely affect U.S. security by destabilizing nuclear deterrence relationships with adversaries and/or by contributing to a competition in nuclear-armed missiles. This Insight focuses on certain strategic stability issues that Congress may consider when providing oversight of or funding for Golden Dome.

item.content:encoded:
PARIS — An acquisition tool that the Pentagon has recently favored now comes with more strings attached following a late October ruling from a federal judge on a Navy drone boat program.

Judge Philip Hadji, who sits on the Federal Court of Claims, asserts the court is a venue to challenge Other Transaction Authorities, providing a check against OTA awards from the Pentagon, according to the Oct. 30 ruling that was unsealed last week.

Other transaction authority, an acquisition tool developed during the space race, has been the funding tool of choice for rapid acquisition across the Defense Department. Under OTAs, the Navy has acquired everything from landing ships to software craft requirements that aren’t covered by the Federal Acquisition Regulation. Functionally, it means the Pentagon isn’t required to announce OTAs or disclose the amount of the awards, unlike traditional contracts.

“OTAs rely on DoD contracting officials to customize the terms and conditions they deem necessary to protect the government’s interests. This flexibility may help DoD attract nontraditional defense contractors that otherwise may not choose to contract with DoD,” reads a 2025 Government Accountability Office report on the tool.

From 2016 to 2024, OTAs grew from $1.8 billion to $18 billion as more prototyping efforts have shifted to the funding model, according to the GAO. The Trump Administration has increased OTAs as part of an overall push for rapid acquisition.

For example, venture capital-backed shipbuilder Saronic has been awarded OTAs for small and medium robotic surface craft and for the traditional LCU-1700 landing ship program.

The Navy’s MUSV program is $2.1 billion and will be funded with OTAs.

Until the ruling, there was no clear venue to challenge the government’s awards.

The case brought by MUSV makers Saildrone and Blue Water Autonomy argued the Navy did not follow its own criteria in how it picked contenders for the MUSV program that used OTAs. As part of the ruling, Hadji found that the Federal Court of Claims has the authority to hear cases protesting an award that would lead to a full program.

Hadji ruled in favor of Saildrone but upheld the Navy’s decision not to advance Blue Water Autonomy.

He said the court “has broad procurement protest jurisdiction over any objection to a solicitation, proposed award, award, or alleged violation of statute or regulation ‘in connection with a procurement or proposed procurement,’ which includes ‘all stages of the process of acquiring property or services, beginning with the process for determining a need for property or services.”

Saildrone will now be reevaluated for the MUSV effort and Hadji ordered a status report on the overall program in 90 days.

“The future of naval warfare will be fought on the water, not in a courtroom,” said Saildrone CEO Richard Jenkins in a statement. ”We are eager to move beyond this litigation and return our entire focus to delivering world-leading maritime autonomy for the US Navy, to help secure America’s future maritime dominance. This ruling is a win for fair competition, for taxpayers, and for national security.”

In a statement, Blue Water Autonomy founder Austin Gray told USNI News, “Blue Water and Saildrone won this argument. This argument was one of three that Blue Water had to win in order to drive corrective action by the Navy.”

What the ruling will do is place more scrutiny on the process, a budget expert with the American Enterprise Institute told USNI News.

“Expansion of bid protest jurisdiction on OTAs at the Federal Court of Claims has a significant potential to destroy OTA authority as a fast alternative to developing new capabilities,” American Enterprise Institute’s Bill Greenwalt told USNI News last month. “At the same time the services contracting organizations seem to think they can load up OTAs with all sorts of traditional [regulation] type clauses, mandates, criteria and requirements and still call it an OTA so they can get a pass by being perceived as being exempt from the protest process.”

The ruling is a recognition that the Navy can’t use OTAs without scrutiny, Greenwalt said.

“Having the [court] slap down the Navy may be productive if it leads to a return to how OTAs are supposed to work by bringing non-traditionals into the market,” he said. “If Navy contracting officers are using the authority as a ruse to eventually award to traditional contractors, which is a distinct possibility in this procurement, then they deserve to be called out on the carpet.”

In a statement to USNI News, the Pentagon said they were aware of the ruling.

“We are aware of the Court of Federal Claims’ ruling in the Blue Water Autonomy/Saildrone matter. The litigation is pending with the Department of Justice and the Department of Navy. We do not comment on ongoing litigation. The Department will review the matter and develop next steps once the litigation is resolved,” reads a statement from a Pentagon spokesperson.

The case has been resolved, but the Defense Department could appeal the ruling. A spokesperson did not respond if the Pentagon would appeal when asked by USNI News.

The ruling comes as OTAs have received increasing criticism in academic circles.

“If lawmakers don’t narrow the authority, they risk sleepwalking the American people into a generation of Pentagon boondoggles,” wrote Julia Gledhill of the Stimson Center in Breaking Defense last month.

Non-traditional defense companies continue to defend the OTA model as effective over the bureaucratic process of Pentagon acquisition, which is governed by the Federal Acquisition Regulation.

“We should just go back to 100 [percent] FAR-based contracts. …said no-one ever,” Blue Water Autonomy founder Gray said in a post on X.
